name: SWE-Gym
description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents. It contains 2,438 real-world task instances, each comprising a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. Tasks are sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories, with pre-configured executable environments and expert-validated test cases. SWE-Gym also includes SWE-Gym Lite (230 instances) for rapid prototyping and SWE-Gym Raw (64,689 instances spanning 358 Python repositories) without executable environments.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang
publisher: PMLR (Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning)
citeAs: Pan, J., Wang, X., Neubig, G., Jaitly, N., Ji, H., Suhr, A., & Zhang, Y. (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267.
rai:dataCollection: SWE-Gym was constructed by identifying Python repositories using SEART GitHub search, filtering for repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors. Task instances were extracted from pull requests using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script. Executable environments were manually configured for 11 repositories, and instances were validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: SWE-Gym Raw instances (64,689) do not contain executable environments or a guarantee that unit tests are effective in evaluating the correctness of a solution. After validation and filtering out failed instances, 2,438 unit-test-validated instances were obtained from 11 repositories.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Real-world GitHub issues and pull requests from 358 Python repositories, filtered using SEART GitHub search. The raw data includes natural language issue descriptions, repository snapshots, and unit tests associated with each pull request.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories created before July 1, 2022 were included. The dataset construction process is described as occurring prior to the paper's publication in 2025.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Instances were versioned by associating them with their respective version numbers and setting up environments version-by-version. Dependencies were manually configured for each task instance using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. SWE-Gym Lite was filtered following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation. Per-instance capping was applied to limit the maximum number of selected samples per task to address data bias.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Repositories were filtered using SEART GitHub search criteria (created before July 1, 2022, >500 stars, >=300 lines of code, >500 pull requests, >100 contributors). Task instances were extracted using SWE-Bench's instance extraction script. Instances were versioned using a generalized SWE-Bench versioning script. Executable environments were set up and validated using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code. Failed instances were filtered out, resulting in 2,438 validated instances. Pre-built Docker images were created for each instance for reproducibility.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors. The process involved manually configuring dependencies for each task instance and validating that the gold patch (human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script. This required approximately 200 human annotation hours. Agent trajectories were labeled as successful or unsuccessful based on whether they passed the unit tests in SWE-Gym.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script; OpenHands remote runtime for parallelized evaluation; Docker images for reproducible environments
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Trajectories were labeled as successful if the agent's solution passed the unit tests. For verifier training, successful and unsuccessful trajectories were balanced by randomly sampling the same amount of unsuccessful trajectories. Per-instance capping was introduced to address bias toward easier tasks in the training dataset. The gap between Pass@k and Best@k metrics indicates imperfect verifier performance and room for improvement in reward modeling.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: SWE-Gym, models, and agent trajectories are publicly released. Pre-built Docker images for each instance are released, totaling 6 TB. The dataset, model weights, agent trajectory data, and training pipeline are all open-sourced.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. Current models are primarily research artifacts and not yet production-ready, but can support critical open-source infrastructure and potentially make software development more accessible. As agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code.
rai:dataBiases: The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern, with pandas comprising nearly one-third of total tasks and bokeh representing only one percent. Tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those in SWE-Bench. Repeated sampling shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, biasing training data toward easier tasks. Manual configuration of environments avoids potential dataset bias from discarding instances with complex dependencies.
rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11 with executable environments), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). Performance is currently limited by the compute budget for sampling rather than the number of tasks. Self-improvement results are modest. The dataset covers only 11 repositories with executable environments out of 358 identified repositories.
rai:dataUseCases: Training language model-based software engineering agents via rejection sampling fine-tuning and reinforcement learning; training verifier/reward models for inference-time scaling; benchmarking and evaluating SWE agent performance; rapid prototyping using SWE-Gym Lite; future research in SWE agent development and automatic dataset synthesis using SWE-Gym Raw.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the paper's authors (researchers at UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, and Apple).
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SWE-Bench's instance extraction script; SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script; SWE-Bench's versioning script; OpenHands remote runtime; SGLang for inference; torchtune for fine-tuning; Unsloth library for LoRA fine-tuning; Docker for containerized environments; GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet for trajectory sampling
